column1: # seance snapshot-name vectors -- the wire protocol's oracle.
#   input     the snapshot SHORT name, the part after the '@'
#   node      the expected node field, or - when the verdict is foreign
#   ts        the expected timestamp,  or - when the verdict is foreign
# Lines beginning with '#' and blank lines are ignored. Nothing else in this
# file is a comment: a '#' inside an input column is part of the input.
# This file is the oracle. Two implementations meet on this grammar -- the
# replication engine that writes names and the status/promote paths that read
# them -- so neither of them gets to be the authority, and a change to the
# parser that these rows do not sanction is a change to the wire protocol.
# "foreign" means ignore-not-error (handoff §2.1): other tools keep snapshots
# in the same datasets, and seance must walk past a name it does not recognise
# without comment and without a non-zero exit.
# The parse runs from the RIGHT. Node names may contain dashes, and one may
# itself end in something that looks like a timestamp; those rows are the
# reason the grammar is specified the way it is, and they are the first rows
# --- boundaries: the node field at its extremes, and the node named after the tool
# A node key may be as long as an operator cares to type, and a fleet whose
# node is literally called 'seance' must still parse: the prefix is stripped
# once, from the left, and the node field is whatever is left of the final
# dash. Both are read from the RIGHT, which is what makes them work at all.
